In the bustling labyrinth of a city mall, a grisly murder sends shockwaves as Xenia is killed with a nail gun, leaving Detective Winston with two perplexing suspects: Van and Wilfred.

Detective Winston had always maintained a level of personal fitness as part of his job. Staying in shape was crucial for catching suspects on foot. But even he was taken aback by the sheer enormity of Van, the local bodybuilder. The rumor in town was that Van had been recently struggling with large debts. The man stood near six and a half feet tall, his enormous physique a testament to the countless hours he obviously spent in the gym, instead of accepting invitations to the various social events.

Winston felt like David meeting Goliath as he marched towards the muscular man. "Hey, Van?" He called out, to which the man gave a mere grunt in response. Several people in the gym watched as the scene unfolded; in this place, Van was a sort of brawny legend who preferred the solitude of his weights over any socializing. Just the other day, a friend had asked him about his dating life with Xenia, but he brushed it aside.

"Detective Winston. I'd like to ask you a few questions," Winston showed his badge. "About Xenia."

Van was taken-aback by the upfrontness of the question. He grunted again, this time out of exasperation. 

"Detective, didn't expect that one coming," he said finally lifting his head to acknowledge the detective. "Alright, shoot."

Winston pulled out his notebook and an envelope from the local hardware store, "Did you take a construction safety course recently?"

"Yeah, I used to build furniture for fun," Van answered in between grunts, continuing his reps, "Safety first and all that."

"And did this fascination with construction lead you to buying a nail gun?" Winston asked, pulling a purchase receipt out of the envelope. "The receipt I found in your wallet indicates you bought the same model used for Xenia's murder."

Van's expression changed for the first time, a small frown appeared on his face. "Yeah, why?"

"There's no easy way to say this..." Winston gathered his words, "but Xenia, she's been killed. She was shot with a nail gun. The same type that you recently bought."

Van's barbell dropped onto the floor with a loud crash. "Xenia is dead?" he asked in disbelief. 

Winston confirmed with a solemn nod. "She recently updated her life insurance policy, which you had changed to make you the sole beneficiary." He added, "The payout would be considerable, enough to solve your debt troubles."

Disbelief crossed Van's face. He ruffled his hair nervously before swiftly changing the topic, "I hit a new record today. 350 pounds."

A change in topic wasn't unusual when dealing with shock, to Winston's experience. He however, decided to dive ahead, "Xenia's will and her life insurance policy, which amounts to a hefty sum of $1.2 million, put a lot of money in your name, Van."

Van swiftly stood from his weight bench, a scowl deepening on his face. "Are you implying I killed her for her money?"

"Just figuring out what happened," Winston calmly replied.

"Well, if that's all detective, you'll have to excuse me. I've got to... digest this information," Van said, storming out of the gym.

Winston watched him leave, noting that for someone who'd just lost someone close, Van seemed to recover pretty fast. He jotted down a final note: 'Van wasn't much for social events, but he certainly had his priorities set on the gym.' With a sigh, he reached for his phone... There was more investigation to be done.

Winston pulled into his usual parking spot at the bustling shopping mall, where Xenia had been found dead. Taking a moment, he observed the familiar sight of storied storefronts and the commotion of shoppers going about their business – everything seemed normal, but its surface was marred by the undercurrent of a sinister act.

Stepping out, Winston headed towards the scene of the crime, where Xenia's body was discovered amongst the kaleidoscope of mall storefronts.

Suddenly, his phone rang. Winston answered it briskly, "This is Winston."

"This is Janet from Dispatch. Got a preliminary report back. The murder weapon was a nail gun... reportedly missing from a nearby construction site." Janet informed him.

"Interesting... thanks, Janet." Winston said before hanging up.

One person in mind, Winston mused, Wilfred, a city lawyer handling the lawsuit against the mall’s recent haphazardly built expansion – he was known to have some construction experience with a reported affinity for nail guns. Funny little detail that used to be an innocence quirk of Wilfred’s. After all, the nail gun was reported missing from Wilfred’s construction project.

Winston walked into the site of construction, observing the works and chaos of a massive project, evidence of Wilfred’s connection with the site.

Later, Winston decided to pay Wilfred a visit. Finding him in his office, Winston pulled out a photo from his coat pocket and tossed it on Wilfred's desk – a grainy shot from a CCTV footage showing Wilfred in the mall at the time of Xenia’s death.

Wilfred squinted at the image, evidently uncomfortable. With his back turned to Winston, working late at his desk, he seemed just as any other lawyer.

"Wilfred, doing some moonlighting at the mall, were you?" Winston asked, his tone casual yet probing.

"I... I do my evening walks there sometimes," Wilfred replied.

Winston pulled out another document from his coat pocket, "You may want to come down to the station, Wilfred. Answer a few questions about your whereabouts last night."

Wilfred hesitated, then nodded, "I understand."

As Winston left Wilfred’s office, he couldn't help wonder about Xenia’s last desperate plead to Wilfred, about specifically taking down the corrupt politician down, waving her damning evidence. As allegations of political scandal were beginning to surround Wilfred, Xenia had somehow been caught in the crossfire. She paid a high price, killed during a time when Wilfred had no alibi, when his whereabouts were unknown to all.

The lawyer’s life slowly gave away a shade that Winston hadn't exactly expected. Packed with political scandal, hurried construction projects, controversial missing nail guns, and unaccounted for times, life was never meant to be this complicated.

Winston closed the car door behind him, a deep sigh escaping him. The case had just begun.

In the hushed sanctity of an ancient temple, the seemingly innocuous corkscrew turns deadly, plunging Detective Winston into a maze of deceit with only two suspects - Xochitl and Martin.

With Olivia's murder still fresh, Winston found himself at the local temple, the gusty air bringing an ominous chill. Instagram photos and notes, discovered by Xochitl, declared that Olivia had intentions to seriously harm Xochitl's sister and ruin her life. Olivia's actions had extended to constant harassment, as per statements from numerous local residents. 

That's when Winston set his eyes on Xochitl for the first time. A town local, known for conducting regular Tarot readings, she was known to have a strong inclination towards rituals and esoteric practices. The temple was often her stage for spiritual enlightenment, which required the uncorking of ritualistic wine bottles with a trusty corkscrew, a habit she had grown accustomed to.

Winston approached her while she was meticulously packing away her Tarot cards, her dark, expressive eyes betraying a myriad of deep emotions. "Are you always this involved in your...ritual practices?" he asked, noting her obvious devotion. "Yes," she responded, her voice barely rising above the rustling of her Tarot cards. "It has become a part of me, something very close to my heart."

Winston paused before asking about her trips. Xochitl's expression faltered a bit as she looked at him, then away. "They happen now and then," she said calmly, swiftly changing the subject to the next upcoming spiritual gathering. Winston noted that her trips were far from listed on her nearby calendar, a fact he filed away on his internal docket.

Conversation shifted, and Xochitl showered her sister with affection. She shared a story of a recent conflict Olivia had with her sister, one laced with threats to ruin her life. The passion with which Xochitl narrated the story was palpable.

As Winston was exiting, he caught sight of various trinkets littered around Xochitl's space. A glance at one of the suitcase tags confirmed it had an origin from a foreign country. He recalls how the locals often gossiped about Xochitl bringing back a new trinket or souvenir from each trip she made, adding to her ever-growing collection. It was the same country that matched one of Xochitl's passport stamps -- a souvenir from her unmarked trips perhaps. The details of her travels remained shrouded in mystery, with Xochitl deftly avoiding deeper conversations about these.

"I'll speak with you soon, Xochitl," Winston affirmed as he left, feeling a complex web of possibilities dissecting in his mind. Curious about the tie between Xochitl, her mysterious trips, the souvenirs and the tragic murder, he was determined to peel back the layers of ambiguity surrounding this case.

In the wake of the unfortunate event at the local temple, Detective Winston flipped through the details of the victims. A familiar sense of dread had come to accompany the name of Olivia – similar to the other women whose investigations he had compiled over time, yet still distinctly unique. It spurred the creeping sensation of a suspected serial killer at large.

“There’s something about this delivery guy…” he murmured, pulling a file, filled with suspicions, on Martin, a package delivery driver. Winston had previously handled several investigations related to Martin for similar incidents, but they had all gone cold. “Is it déjà vu?”

He shuffled through the documents in Martin's file. The delivery man, as per his employer’s statement, made regular visits to the temple for his deliveries, which interestingly enough, had also happened on the fateful day Olivia was found dead. Today, he was scheduled to deliver a package to none other than Olivia herself.

As Winston read further, he scratched the stubble on his chin, remembering a tidbit he had come across in one of the previous investigations. Martin had this... peculiar method of opening packages, using a corkscrew. Yes, a corkscrew of all things. And that was a part of his regular equipment, he would carry it with him every day.

Quirkily, during an early afternoon surveillance encounter upon one of his visits at the temple on the very day of the murder, Martin was seen carrying his odd tool, the corkscrew.

"It's ironic, don't you think?" One of his fellow officers had remarked dryly. "Our potential serial killer and his corkscrew."

Winston refrained from comment, remembering the discrepancies that had led those cases to grow cold. Several of them were left inconclusive - always touch and go - with evidence that went around in circles but never quite completed the picture.

As he went through his notes, Winston noticed another uncanny resemblance - Olivia was quite similar in appearance to the past victims; young, brunette, and striking eyes.

Fingers drumming against the cool, polished surface of his wooden desk, Winston reviewed Martin’s work log. It noted the driver was prescheduled enough to have him at the temple around the suspected time of Olivia’s demise that day. With furrowed brows, he made note of the temple's solitary condition during the time - not another soul around.

Too many coincidences and not enough clarity. Winston sighed heavily, clicking his pen shut. The more things unravelled, the more they seemed convoluted. But he knew better than to pinpoint connections. For now, it was about gathering facts, no matter how cryptic.

In a grimly lit motel room, Detective Winston finds himself face to face with Adam's charred remains and two potential suspects: Gregory and Alfred. The murder weapon? An unlikely and gruesome choice, a flamethrower.


Detective Winston noticed Alfred almost immediately at the motel tournament. Not only because Alfred was a stellar athlete known for his flamethrower skills, but also due to his nonchalant display of his large, mysterious tool bag. This was particularly noticeable each time Winston spotted him leaving the motel on full moon nights, ready for a game. 

Winston approached Alfred after he ended yet another victorious game under the full moon. "Alfred, right?" Winston diplomatically asked. 

"Yep, that's me." Alfred replied, a hint of pride mirroring in his words. The detectable pride wasn't out of place considering Alfred always seemed to score the winning point on the nights the moon was full.

"And you always play on full moon nights, right?" Winston inquired, relying on his prior knowledge of the tournament's nature.

Alfred answered, chuckling a bit to himself, "A little superstitious, I guess. I do always seem to score the winning point when the moon's full."

As he spoke, Winston became aware of an oversized tool bag resting near Alfred's feet. He couldn't ignore the temptation of questioning, "That's a pretty big bag you got there Alfred, what do you use that for?"

Alfred paused, "Well.., it's for my flamethrower. They don't just hand those out to anyone, you know. I'm a pro at handling them."

Later that evening, the police received a tip about the tool bag. Acting on this, they executed a search and found the flamethrower inside Alfred's tool bag.

The mention of a flamethrower took Winston aback, considering its relation to the crime, but he returned his focus to their conversation. "I heard the motel hosts your team's meetings, correct?"

Alfred nodded, "That's right, usually in Adam’s room. He'd let us use his room because it was more spacious."

Noticing a key on a hoop attached to Alfred's bag, Winston asked, "And that key, would that be to Adam's room?"

Taken by surprise, Alfred replied, "Yeah, I suppose it is... he'd given me and the other team members a spare. We had the tournament here. Every full moon night you'd see me leaving with this bag and the key to Adam's room to hit the field."

Winston remembered confirming that very fact from the official schedule he had reviewed at the precinct. Winston excused himself promising to catch the next game. As he left, he kept a watchful eye on Alfred, particularly when he was set to leave for the games on the nights of the full moon, and his unusually conspicuous tool bag.

Winston sat at the corner of the dimly lit motel bar nursing a whiskey neat, his eyes periodically scanning the room in sharp, calculated movements. Earlier in the day, he had confirmed with his latest suspect, Gregory, that this was indeed the motel where Adam had been staying the night of the murder.

Turning his gaze to the last row of whiskey bottles on the backlit shelf, he saw the reflection of a familiar figure making his way to the counter. Interestingly, when he'd questioned the locals in his investigation, they'd claimed to have seen Gregory nearby the motel bar on the night Adam was killed. Seeing Gregory now in the same bar seemed to affirm their claims.

Gregory was an older man, a veteran, disciplined and proud. His home was a menagerie of functional military memorabilia, everything from gun replicas to deactivated grenades. Among his collection was an impressively well-maintained flamethrower, understandably a surreal sight. But it was common among veterans like Gregory to go through great lengths to preserve the physical memories of their service. Gregory himself had been trained in the use of such weapons during his time in the military.

"Hey, what's a whiskey neat run you in a place like this?" Winston asked, breaking the silence that had instinctively shrouded Gregory at the sight of him.

The barmaid laughed, glancing up at the chalkboard behind her. "You're holding it, detective."

"Ah, that I am." Winston responded, leaning in closer.

Gregory had known Adam was staying at this motel. In fact, it was Adam himself that told him so. However, the two of them weren't what you'd call good friends. A distinct air of tension traced the edges of their relationship.

Adam was privy to a secret of Gregory's. A secret that, if revealed, could sour Gregory's reputation beyond repair. It wasn't just idle gossip either. Adam had managed to procure evidence of Gregory's transgressions.

No, they weren't friends. Gregory had offered Adam money to keep his secret. Instead of growing quiet out of greed, Adam was currently residing in the morgue as the latest puzzle for Winston.

Despite the severity of Gregory's secret, it was clear that there was more to the matter. This was simply one part of a larger, more intricate tapestry. A single lead in the looming, grey landscape of Winston's ongoing investigation into Adam's murder.

Winston finished his whiskey and slammed the empty glass onto the bar, rising from his seat and stretching. It was time to return to his never-ending game of interviews and detective work. He cast one last glance at the mirror behind the bar, his eyes lingering on the reflection of Gregory.

In the heart of a bustling fitness center, Heidi's life was abruptly silenced by a shotgun's blast; now it's up to the astute Detective Winston to round up suspects Grace and Chester and unravel the threads of this complex murder mystery.

Winston studied Grace's appearance as she labored over the dismantling of her shotgun, a routine she performed with a kind of measured grace that only came with practice.

"I take it hunting is a regular hobby of yours, Grace?" he asked. She straightened her back and brushed a lock of hair from her eyes, her hands still loosely holding the dismantled firearm. She nodded.

"It's tradition. Heidi and I would always go out into the wilderness, me with my nine-two shotgun, her with her ridiculous tin of marshmallows. I remember she'd always be the one who'd leave, while I'd stay at the fire, peering into the forest, not returning to the tent." Grace chuckled, but her smile didn't reach her eyes. "Even when we were out here, pushing fitness, she was looking out for safety."

"And you had a mutual workout routine both of you followed?" Winston questioned.

"Yes, every day like clockwork." She sighed. "But I convinced Heidi to change it. I argued it was safer, better for her. That night she was murdered, she implemented the change."

Winston looked at her, his sharp eyes noticing the glimmers of distress in hers. "Could that change have caused her to meet her killer?"

"She started seeing someone. I thought it was best if we changed the time, to throw off this new person. But she didn't listen..." Her voice held a slight edge, possessive almost.

As she related the details about her trips with Heidi, Winston noticed her rain-soaked hiking boots, mud-streaked pants, and her tired eyes.

"Looks like you've been out there yourself today?" he gestured at her appearance.

"Busy day," Grace responded curtly, her gaze never leaving the shotgun she was now starting to reassemble. "I usually got up the earliest. Not much point in sleeping when there's hunting to be done. The guys in the camp aren't morning people anyway."

"I see," Winston muttered, "You two, you worked out together frequently, didn't you?" 

"Heidi's the one who introduced me to working out at the fitness center. We would even do so late at night, just us, a lot of sweat and a hell of a lot of heavy lifting." She smiled at the thought, her eyes glossing over with a mixture of remembrance and grief. 

Winston nodded, scribbled down a few lines in his notepad and thanked her for her time. There was still so much to understand, so much to link together.

Sunlight filtered in through the windows of the fitness center, casting long shadows on the equipment and machines scattered around the vast room. In the corner of the spacious gym, Chester was spotted, tending to some weights when detective Winston walked in.

Chester, slight in stature, belied his physical prowess as a jockey. His wiry exterior seemed incongruent with the voracious power emanated by his presence. "Hello Chester," Winston began, his gruff voice noticeably contrasting with the calmness of the gym.

"Detective Winston, isn't it?" Chester replied with ease, his demeanor not showing a single shred of surprise or fear. Just two weeks ago, Chester had started his new gig at the fitness center, partly to make some extra bucks and partly to maintain his fitness routine. It wasn't surprising to Winston that Chester would frequently show up right when Heidi, an active member of the gym, was last seen alive.

Just when he had started to become regular at the gym, murmurs among Chester's gang had grown louder. They've started questioning his loyalties, not convinced that his regular visits to the gym were purely for maintaining his fitness.  

Their subtle talk was interrupted by the loud reverberations of gunshots in the distant background. Chester, an avid hunter, often flexed his shooting skills at the range nearby after winding up work at the gym.

"You like to shoot, huh?" Winston casually pointed towards the direction of the gun shot sounds. "Yeah. Helps take the edge off," Chester replied, a faint smile appeasing his otherwise-hardened face.

The conversation gradually led them to Heidi, a brave woman who had recently made criticisms about Chester's gang at a local town meeting. Their illegal activities were an open secret in town, countered only by the fear they instilled in those who dared to oppose. Heidi was the latest in the list, her fate tying in with an unfortunate coincidence: Chester's gang members are known to carry shotguns, the same kind that ended her life. 

Detective Winston and Chester finally diverged to their respective routines. The detective's mind was buzzing with theories, but his face was an ocean of calm. He had gathered the facts. The story had to be spun. His job could not be influenced by hasty conclusions... not when the facts all led to one presumable as intimidating as Chester.

In a shocking twist of events, Faith has been gruesomely murdered by a lawnmower in her own kitchen and now, Detective Winston must unravel the tangled web of suspicion entangling Clyde and Paul.

Detective Winston strolled into the barber shop, glancing casually around at the collections of stuffed animals that peppered the shop floor. In the very middle of the shop was an imposing stuffed grizzly bear, imposing its dead presence on the area.

Paul was busy with a customer, chatting away about the rare bird species in the case next to the register. The customer, just one of many who had complained about Paul's excessive taxidermy talks, looked painfully bored, his eyes glazed over as Paul prattled on about the bird's curved beak, delicately preserved feathers and where he had obtained such a unique specimen.

Winston leaned by the counter and asked Paul, nonchalantly, "Do you do the occasional yard work in between haircuts?" 

"All the time," Paul responded, finishing up with the disgruntled customer and turning to Winston, not pausing his monologue about another piece of taxidermy. "Yard work helps to make ends meet. I was actually at Faith's place just before...well, you know. I even had access to her kitchen whenever I needed a glass of water."

That seemed to shut him up momentarily, a somber silence filling the barbershop. Winston looked at him, intrigued. 

"It's none of my business, Paul, but I heard your barbershop's been on the rocks lately. Times are tough, huh? Even heard you had to borrow from some loan sharks.", he tried to sound casual.

"Yeah, it's been rough. Lost a few customers, owe some money here and there," Paul’s gaze wandered to the floor, swallowed by the fear of the loan shark's due date.

Winston looked around and made an offhand remark. "Maybe all this taxidermy is scaring them off?"

Paul defended his role, "People don't understand! It's an art." His placid face turned dark, "And nowadays people don’t understand art."

A minute passed before he asked, "Can I use your bathroom, Paul?"

"Sure, Detective, right through that door and to the left.", he said, his gaze falling onto a corner of the shop. 

He let himself into the bathroom, noticing its cleanliness. Paul was meticulous, that was clear. 

As he left, he asked if he could see the papers for Faith's insurance policy. 

"Why?" Paul’s face tensed up at the question. 

"Just routine procedure, Paul." Winston lied.

Paul hesitated before conceding, and then he handed over the papers. Winston skimmed through them, taking a mental note of the surprisingly high coverage and finding that Paul was indeed listed as the sole beneficiary.

Looking straight into Paul's eyes he finally said, "You know, Paul, sometimes it pays to be the policy holder’s primary beneficiary."

Paul looked back at him, pale, but with a composed poker face as he uttered his last denial of the day, "I had nothing to do with Faith’s death, Detective Winston.”

Winston found himself examining a scene in Faith's kitchen, evidence strewn everywhere he looked. He took backward steps, tripping and almost falling on an oddly placed lawnmower at the end of the room. The heavy machine was terribly out of place and hinted at a violent use he found hard to reconcile with the peaceful intent for which it was designed; surely, only someone accustomed to wielding weapons could have wielded it so. 

"Since when has gardening become an indoor activity?" He muttered under his breath, the strange possibility of the lawnmower having been used as a murder weapon intriguing him.

A neighborhood visitor claimed they spotted Clyde, a man whose name popped up frequently during interviews, in Faith's kitchen at the time of the murder. His visit raised suspicions as Faith's husband, Greg, was out of town.

Clyde had just been recently subjected to a publicly organized demotion in his military profession, an event planned by Faith herself. This was a peculiar twist instead of an expected promotion. The profound humiliation Clyde underwent was palpable. Faith didn't just demote him; she ridiculed his past failures in front of friends and colleagues. 

Then Winston found Clyde in his backyard, tirelessly mowing his large lawn. Given his military background, the sight of him comfortably handling the heavy gardening equipment was no surprise. Clad in an army green tank top and dirt smeared jeans, he resembled a typical middle-aged soldier.

"I hear you were out here mowing your lawn yesterday as well," Winston ventured, trying to sound casual.

Clyde simply nodded, "It takes a while, you see. Large lawn and all."

They chatted about his daily chores, Clyde even admitted his preference for maintaining his own lawn. As they spoke of his military background, Clyde shared that he had extensive training in handling various types of weapons and machinery. The mention of this made Winston think of the misplaced lawnmower at Faith's house. 

As the subject shifted towards the night of the murder, Clyde confessed knowing Greg would be away. There was an eerie ease in which he knew about Faith's daily routine, which would have left her alone in the kitchen.

"It was an open secret. Faith loved to bake, known to everyone in the neighborhood," Clyde said, his tone devoid of any resentment.

Winston, before he left, broached the topic of his demotion ceremony. A grimace appeared on Clyde's face at the mention of Faith's sly ploy during his promotion.

"That was... regrettable," he muttered, "Faith had her fun ridiculing me. I swore I would get even for such humiliation."

As Winston reached for the gate, Clyde, playing with the freshly mowed grass, added, "Detective, she didn't just embarrass me, she made it personal. That day will forever be etched in my memory."

Driving back downtown, Winston pondered over the circumstances surrounding Faith's unexpected demise and the uncanny presence of a lawnmower.

In a shocking twist of events, Faith has been gruesomely murdered by a lawnmower in her own kitchen and now, Detective Winston must unravel the tangled web of suspicion entangling Clyde and Paul.

As Winston entered a well-kept home, he observed Clyde, an army man of some years, meticulously dusting and straightening up everything in sight. Checking his watch, Winston observed the room to be empty of people except for himself and Clyde. It was a known fact Clyde only did his cleaning when there was no one else in the room, a peculiar habit of his. "Evening, Clyde," he said by way of greeting.

"Detective," Clyde returned, his face neutral. His large lawn, recently mowed, was visible through the window. The neighbours had seen him mowing it just yesterday, a job required a heavy machine like a lawnmower which, due to its aggressiveness, demanded some level of foundational weapon training.

Winston gazed around the room, making a mental note of the pristine condition of the house. "You keep a fine home," Winston commented, to which Clyde merely offered a grunt of response and continued his clean-up. He knew the moment guests would arrive, he'd start cleaning again from scratch in his usual obsessive way.

Winston then recalled what some prior guests had mentioned, they noticed certain items of theirs were missing when they left Clyde's house. He quoted an instance, “Mr. Johnson, your neighbour across the street told me about his missing gloves after he visited your house last time, have you noticed it by any chance?”

Clyde's face stiffened, "I don't know anything about that." But Winston noted down this peculiar fact as a part of his ongoing investigation.

Winston Revolved back to the event driving all this, the promotion ceremony where Faith publicly tore Clyde's reputation to shreds. She ridiculed Clyde's failures in front of many familiar faces causing him an unbearable public humiliation.

“Must’ve indeed been rough for you, being humiliated by Faith in front of everyone at your promotion ceremony,” Winston prodded, causing Clyde to stop his cleaning abruptly. 

“You know, a man can only take so much humiliation," Winston mused, seemingly thoughtful. 

“Oh, I intend to get back at her, in my own way," Clyde promised, his tone carried a chilling promise of revenge for Faith's public humiliation. 

Winston observed Clyde for a moment longer, then rose. "Thank you for your time, soldier." The air around them remained heavy with tension as Winston took his leave. Clyde resumed his cleaning, in the same methodical way he had been seen to do, especially when the room was devoid of people.
   
The formerly unsolved pondering over Clyde's peculiar habit of cleanliness and guests’ missing items seemed to fall into perspective as Winston left the house. Clyde’s indomitable spirit of cleanliness and the mysterious case of the missing items could possibly be related, and with his revenge plans, it was fair to say that Winston's investigation was still far from being concluded.

Winston stood in the quiet, domestic confines of Faith's kitchen, the peculiar scent of freshly cut grass now forever associated with the grim sight that lay before him. His gaze shifted towards the adjacent tool shed, the door slightly ajar, wherein lay the murder weapon, a lawnmower of all things. 

A grimace etched itself across his face as the details replayed in his mind, the cards dealt out complex and interwoven. 

Stepping away from the grisly tableau, he hopped into his car and headed toward a nearby barbershop. The sign flickered in the early evening light, appropriately named, 'Paul's Barber Shop'. The shop was all but empty, a lone barber stood, idly whittling his time away by cleaning a pair of scissors. 

"Help you with something?" His voice echoed throughout the empty shop. 

"I'm Winston, I work with the local force. You wouldn't happen to be Paul, would you?" Winston probed. 

The man just nodded, his expression hardly changing but for the most minute hint of incredulity, as he replied, "Yeah...I am Paul. Something I can do for you, detective?"

Winston gave him a cursory once-over, noting the man's weary demeanor, "I'm sure you're awfully busy, but I'd appreciate a few minutes of your time. You knew Faith, didn't you?" 

Paul maintained his stolid expression, his reply crisp and composed, "Yeah, I knew Faith...quite well as a matter of fact. Been tending to her lawn a bit here and there, alongside my barber duties. She even let me use her bathroom once." 

"So, you would've had fairly regular access to her kitchen... The crime scene?", Winston asked casually.

"Yeah, sure. Actually, that's where she'd serve me sweet tea while I took a break from yard work", Paul said, while sharpening the blade of his razor.

As Paul continued his maintenance routine of the various paraphernalia around him, something clicked in Winston’s mind. Blades... a lawnmower, scissors, razors. All need maintenance, all have blades, and then it struck him. All require a sharp edge for their tasks.

Winston thanked Paul, confirming his appointment for a shave the next day, and retreated under the gaze of the man's cold, money-grubbing eyes. Intentions masked under the facade of a simple barber, tired of his failing shop, tired of life's less-charitable hands, and potentially desperate enough to resort to the unthinkable. His mounting debts with the loan sharks were no secret, after all.

On the way back to his office, Winston made a call, ordering an audit into Faith’s financials. Among her insurance documents, he located the policy Faith had recently taken out - its coverage unusually high. This observation was further perturbed by the paperwork revealing that Paul was listed as the sole beneficiary. 

The reflections of the streetlights illuminated the clues that strewn around Winston’s path like breadcrumbs. A web woven thick with secrecy, desperation, and death. The puzzle was not complete, but the edges were beginning to take shape. Faith's death... Paul's desperation. There was more than met the eye in this grim puzzle.

In the eerie silence of the swamp, Jess was brutally murdered with a sai, leaving Detective Winston sorting through a mire of secrets and lies involving two prime suspects - Leona and Freya.

The muggy air of the swamp, with its accompanying sounds of buzzing insects and distant croaks of frogs, was a strange backdrop to a brutal crime. Winston's face took on a grim expression as he squinted his eyes against the setting sun, trying to piece together the final gruesome moments of Jess. Found dead near the swamp, the victim's pale hand still clutched a crumpled VIP pass to the recent concert. The singer, Leona, was the main attraction.

Deep in thought, Winston absentmindedly thumbed the murder weapon, a well-crafted sai. The sai was brand new, still wearing the faint scent of the store – it was witty of Leona to buy it so recently... Leona's sai... that was found at the scene. With this new piece of information, he decided to pay the singer a visit during her late-night martial arts class.

Entering the practice room, Winston noticed Leona in the middle of an intense sparring session. Her instructor watched with clear admiration as she dodged blows, her expression intense and focused. She slid into stroke, parrying with a level of expertise that implied countless hours of training. The instructor had remarked on her swift improvement with the sa, speculating on the freshness of her acquisition.

After the session, catching her breath with graceful composure, Leona crossed the floor to speak with Winston. As they talked, a subtle shift towards true crime came over their conversation. The sparkle in Leona's eye contrasted against the seriousness of the subject matter. It was clear she was comfortable, almost enthusiastic, addressing crime scenarios, drawing similarities to real events in the documentaries she frequently watched and wrote about. 

As they walked through the venue, Winston observed Leona's possessions, pausing over what appeared to be a well-worn notebook filled with notes upon notes on various crime documentaries. Intriguingly, Winston remembered another reference to this notebook from an event-goer at a recent documentary screening he had attended. He had seen the same notebook in Leona’s hand as she bought her new sai and scribbled away fervently while the documentary ran. 

Winston remarked on the close proximity of the concert venue – only a stone’s throw away from the swamp. Leona explained the choice, explaining how she loved the allure of the swamp during night, something atmospheric and eerie about the location that added a unique edge to her concerts... 

"She headed towards the swamp... after the concert, going towards the place she loved." The innocent statement caught Winston by surprise. He had stumbled upon someone who had noticed Jess, after Leona's performance, walk blissfully towards the swamp, clutching her VIP pass – the scene of her untimely death.

As Detective Winston thanked Leona for her time, he looked back at the singer, her recently purchased sai cradled in her forearm skillfully as if it were an extension of her own body. Winston couldn't quite shake off the strange sensation that washed over him. Returning to the stillness of his own vehicle, not yet ready to move on, he just sat there under the starlight, trying to make sense of the eerie dance between the facts that were slowly crafting the narrative to this murder. The story had many more veiled layers waiting to be discovered — and some heavy curtains waiting to be lifted.

Winston found himself standing in Freya's living room, his eyes quickly falling on a display case filled with various medieval weapons including the peculiar missing spot of a sai. Freya positioned herself beside Winston, noting his interest in her unique collection, "Those ais hold a special place in my heart. A reminder of my martial arts training back in the day. Even last week, I was at the dojo practicing with my favorite, a sai."

"Interesting," Winston hummed, a non-committal sound as he mentally filed away the information. He peered at the open spot in the case shaping a sai- the exact style like the weapon found in Jess and seemingly missing from the collection. He remembered the local authorities report about a matching weapon disappearing recently. 

Shifting his focus back on Freya, Winston decided to delve deeper. "And you frequent the local dojo, am I correct?" 

"Yes," Freya piped, curious. "I was there just last week."

"And Jess," Winston moved on. "You seem to have spent quite a sum to gain some insight on her."

Flustered, Freya breathed heavily, "Yes, I hired a private investigator. Jess started playing games, bragging about dirt she claimed to have on me."

"How does bird-watching tie into these games?" Winston questioned, casually dropping a seemingly unrelated question.

Taken aback, Freya chuckled awkwardly, "Well detective, I do frequent the swamp near here to observe the local birdlife. And yes, my car was indeed spotted parked there recently."

Seizing the moment, Winston probed, "So you would be quite familiar with navigating the swamplands then?" 

Freya gritted her teeth, "Yes, Detective. As I said, I often go there. My father taught me how to navigate those swamps."

Next he opened his folder, producing the letter meant for the local paper, written by Jess. Winston watched as Freya's reactions shifted from surprise to anger, to a controlled calm. It spoke volumes more than her carefully composed words, "Jess threw accusations left and right, yes. I asked our mutual friends to intervene, to convince her against disclosing these…misconceptions. But, you see, I also heard something disturbing about her. A woman fitting my description was seen heading towards the swamps.” Freya finished, eyes shimmering with unexpected tears.

Winston took a moment to consider her words, nodding slowly, "You've been very helpful, Freya. Thank you." His mind still picking on the revelations, the omissions, the twitches, keeping him aware that the game's just begun.

When the silver screen flickered with an unexpected explosion, claiming the life of innocent Chloe, seasoned Detective Winston stepped in to unravel the deadly scandal entwining suspects Ruby and Roscoe.

Stepping through the bustling crime scene of a movie theater, Winston drew deeply on his cigarette, turning over the few facts he had. It was a terrible scene involving a grenade explosion, a midnight movie, and a tragedy. Winston ran a hand over his tired face as he recollected the events of the night. The victim, Chloe, had invited Ruby, a local psychic with a unique talent of foreseeing dangerous situations in her visions, to the movies. In the past, these visions had often involved violent scenes where weapons like grenades were used, a dangerous gift she suspected was influenced by her military background.

They'd stayed until the late night showing ended, and witnesses mentioned they were the last to leave. They also confirmed that none other individuals were seen entering or exiting the theater. 

Winston made his way to the torn-up cinema, stooping to look at the grenaded remains. The air was still heavy with the acrid residue of the explosion. Ruby, the psychic. Ruby, the military veteran. He suppressed a shudder as he thought about the fatalities she might have presaged in her past, with the shadow of a grenade always lingering in her visions, all too accurate.

In situations like these, she could have known how to handle a grenade, her service in the military would have ensured that. He had heard about this psychic's history. Ruby's accuracy was unsettling... Her record of predicting family tragedies had created an odd mix of fear and respect amongst her kin. They were a superstitious lot, some even believed that her visions were causing the very catastrophes she prophesied.

Winston beckoned an officer over, borrowing his notepad and pen to jot down some reminders. Ruby was last seen with Chloe. Ruby went to her brother’s house after the movie - The brother, who also happens to be an arms dealer.

Winston made his way to Ruby's apartment for an interview. Ruby had a feral look about her - her argument with her mother had clearly shaken her. She had decided to break off contact with her family after that blowout. Both of them seemed to be quite stubborn.

"Ruby," Winston began, "Can you tell me about the last time you saw Chloe?" He asked, his steely gaze fixing on her. 

"Yes, Detective. We watched a movie together. It ran late, we both stayed until the end." Ruby replied.

"And after the movie?" Winston probed.

"I... I went to visit my brother. He sells... various products. I remember when we played with toy soldiers as children..." Ruby’s voice trailed off, an odd glint in her eyes. 

Keeping his inquisitive gaze steady, Winston made his leave, leaving Ruby and her prophecies, often echoing with the sound of pin-pulled grenades, alone with the evening shadows.

Winston rubbed his temples as he sifted through the mountain of paperwork on his desk. What a way to spend his Sunday, pouring over case files and suspect lists. He moved onto the next file on his desk: Roscoe, an astrophysicist by day, apparent drug addict by night. 

His astrophysics job had Roscoe planted in a military base, which was known to have an arsenal that included grenades, for research purposes. Here, he utilized his broad scientific background including physics and chemistry. Although he normally processed information in a meticulous and scientific manner, witness testimonies painted a different picture altogether. Apparently, Roscoe had been acting erratically lately. Having a quick look at his employee records, Winston saw a slew of complaints piled up within the last few weeks. 

Roscoe's troubles found their way outside of the workplace, into a small apartment where he was the tenant. When the police were called for a noise complaint, they found drug paraphernalia scattered across the living room. Surely, his military career would see its last days if word got out. 

Winston sighed, leaning back in his chair, skimming through his notes. He paused at the mention of a late-night movie. Chloe, the unfortunate victim, had been Roscoe's unsuspecting companion in the dark theater. Just as the opening credits rolled, her life had been cut short by a grenade. 

Witness statements gathered at the scene confirmed that Roscoe had purchased a ticket for the same movie screening just moments before it began. Someone had seen him enter the theater, seemingly in a hurry. 

"These cases just keep getting trickier," Winston muttered to himself, downing another cup of coffee. His eyes moved to another statement, this time by one of Chloe's friends. It seemed that Chloe was about to report Roscoe's drug addiction to his superiors.

Winston called Roscoe's workplace. "Is that Roscoe's current position?" he asked the person on the other end. "Have you noticed anything... odd about his behavior lately?" He listened carefully to the responses, his face impassive.

"No further questions," Winston said as he bid goodbye and hung up the office phone. He then picked up another folder from the desk, ready to tackle the next round of information.

When fitness enthusiast Uma is ominously murdered with a vial of acid at her local gym, it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to unravel the mystery between the two prime suspects, Irving and Addison.

Detective Winston was indoors on another stifling California afternoon. His attention was fixed on the Irving case, a case that kept him on his toes for several days now. A screenwriter suspected in the murder of a fellow gym goer. He couldn’t help but feel the increasing pressure of the time crunch.

Irving was not an ordinary man. Winston had discovered from the interviews and police records that the guy particularly had some weird habits. Irving, it seemed, was battling insomnia and was unable to sleep in his own home at night. During these restless nights, he would busy himself with his notebooks. Often, he was seen at the fitness center, sketching intriguing symbols into his notebook, which he always carried along with his pencil. He would leave home with these immediately after sunset.

One specific detail that struck the detective was Irving's fascination with themes and symbols of the past, particularly those formed by ancient gravestones. These ancient symbols were found in notations and sketches strewn across his notebooks. It was curious to Winston how an old world art found a home in the hands of a modern screenwriter.

His insomniac late-night habits weren't the only thing that raised suspicions, though. Irving also was a member at the same fitness center Uma frequented, spotted regularly training late into the night. The very same fitness center that was the scene of the crime. The records substantiated his presence late on the night of the murder. Like the deceased Uma, he seemed to utilized the solitude that the near-empty gym provided, allowing him ample time alone.

The lines on Winston's forehead became more pronounced as he read on. He found a strange connection between both Uma's and Irving's lives. Not only did they work out at the same gym, but they also shared a professional conflict. Reports indicated that Uma had discovered Irving's success was largely built on her own work which he'd plagiarized. Fearing public humiliation and the definite demise of his screenwriting career, Irving had a lot to lose. To make matters worse for Irving, Uma, the aggrieved, had threatened to expose his deceit to the public.

The tension of the case was truly weighing on Winston. He sighed, leaning back from his desk. Questions in his mind demanded answers that weren't there yet. So, he decided to continue with the investigation, waiting for the breakthrough that would add some clarity to the clouded picture. He had a late-night meeting with the prime suspect, Irving, in the pipeline. It was indeed time to probe further and extract some answers from the silence of the night.

Detective Winston admired the modern glow of the fitness center that served as his next stop in the investigation. The thudding of footfalls on running machines, the humming of weight machines, and the faint scent of sweat and disinfectant whispered of a place that had teetered on the edge of life and death.

"Lookin' to join?" came a voice from behind him. He languidly turned to find Addison, the local trainer.

"No. Detective Winston, on official police business," he presented his badge.

The sour taste of surprise was evident on Addison's face, "We're an excellent gym with a friendly vibe; it's a shame. You don't say, a detective?"

"I've checked the fitness center security cameras," Winston watched as Addison pressed his lips together, "Noticed you were entering the gym shortly before time of Uma's death."

Addison placed a hand on a weight machine, lowering his gaze to his feet. "Uma? You mean my client, Uma? We were scheduled for a training session that day."

Winston opened his notebook, scanning his notes, "You have a background in chemistry, is that right?"

Addison looked up from his shoes, "Yeah, I even teach it at the high school. Possess a chemistry degree and recently purchased a chemistry set for demonstration."

"Interesting. The set contains vials of acid, science class protocol?" Winston asked, his brow furrowing.

"Absolutely, controlled experiments to teach risk and safety," Addison said, transported into the world of academia. The detective noticed a flicker in Addison’s expression as he continued to speak but brushed it off, it meant nothing yet.

A few people from the gym had crowded around now. They watched as Winston asked, "Can you recall Uma saying anything about the honesty of the staff or maybe about any missing equipment?"

"Well," Addison began, rubbing his neck, "Uma did once vouch for me, said I was honest and commendable, a good character, you know." He looked around the room and swallowed. "And yes, she did mention once about missing equipment. Unfortunately, she also stumbled upon some CCTV footage of me taking some expensive equipment. I had intended to return it, it was a mistake. "

As Winston watched the gym members disperse, he looked back at Addison. "So, Uma caught you stealing from the fitness center. That must've been uncomfortable for you. It surfaced in the investigation that fitness equipment has been reported missing recently. Uma seemed to have discovered the theft."

Addison suddenly seemed to find the floor tiles fascinating. "Uma was a good woman," he said quietly. "It's a shame what happened to her."

"Agreed," Winston replied, closing his notebook. "Keep a clear schedule, Addison. We'll be in touch."

As Winston exited the gym he took one more glance at Addison through the large glass panes. Cold air nipped at his face and Winston pondered the car ride back to the station.

“Must’ve indeed been rough for you, being humiliated by Faith in front of everyone at your promotion ceremony,” Winston prodded, causing Clyde to stop his cleaning abruptly. 

“You know, a man can only take so much humiliation," Winston mused, seemingly thoughtful. 

“Oh, I intend to get back at her, in my own way," Clyde promised, his tone carried a chilling promise of revenge for Faith's public humiliation. 

Winston observed Clyde for a moment longer, then rose. "Thank you for your time, soldier." The air around them remained heavy with tension as Winston took his leave. Clyde resumed his cleaning, in the same methodical way he had been seen to do, especially when the room was devoid of people.
   
The formerly unsolved pondering over Clyde's peculiar habit of cleanliness and guests’ missing items seemed to fall into perspective as Winston left the house. Clyde’s indomitable spirit of cleanliness and the mysterious case of the missing items could possibly be related, and with his revenge plans, it was fair to say that Winston's investigation was still far from being concluded.

Winston stood in the quiet, domestic confines of Faith's kitchen, the peculiar scent of freshly cut grass now forever associated with the grim sight that lay before him. His gaze shifted towards the adjacent tool shed, the door slightly ajar, wherein lay the murder weapon, a lawnmower of all things. 

A grimace etched itself across his face as the details replayed in his mind, the cards dealt out complex and interwoven. 

Stepping away from the grisly tableau, he hopped into his car and headed toward a nearby barbershop. The sign flickered in the early evening light, appropriately named, 'Paul's Barber Shop'. The shop was all but empty, a lone barber stood, idly whittling his time away by cleaning a pair of scissors. 

"Help you with something?" His voice echoed throughout the empty shop. 

"I'm Winston, I work with the local force. You wouldn't happen to be Paul, would you?" Winston probed. 

The man just nodded, his expression hardly changing but for the most minute hint of incredulity, as he replied, "Yeah...I am Paul. Something I can do for you, detective?"

Winston gave him a cursory once-over, noting the man's weary demeanor, "I'm sure you're awfully busy, but I'd appreciate a few minutes of your time. You knew Faith, didn't you?" 

Paul maintained his stolid expression, his reply crisp and composed, "Yeah, I knew Faith...quite well as a matter of fact. Been tending to her lawn a bit here and there, alongside my barber duties. She even let me use her bathroom once." 

"So, you would've had fairly regular access to her kitchen... The crime scene?", Winston asked casually.

"Yeah, sure. Actually, that's where she'd serve me sweet tea while I took a break from yard work", Paul said, while sharpening the blade of his razor.

As Paul continued his maintenance routine of the various paraphernalia around him, something clicked in Winston’s mind. Blades... a lawnmower, scissors, razors. All need maintenance, all have blades, and then it struck him. All require a sharp edge for their tasks.

Winston thanked Paul, confirming his appointment for a shave the next day, and retreated under the gaze of the man's cold, money-grubbing eyes. Intentions masked under the facade of a simple barber, tired of his failing shop, tired of life's less-charitable hands, and potentially desperate enough to resort to the unthinkable. His mounting debts with the loan sharks were no secret, after all.

On the way back to his office, Winston made a call, ordering an audit into Faith’s financials. Among her insurance documents, he located the policy Faith had recently taken out - its coverage unusually high. This observation was further perturbed by the paperwork revealing that Paul was listed as the sole beneficiary. 

The reflections of the streetlights illuminated the clues that strewn around Winston’s path like breadcrumbs. A web woven thick with secrecy, desperation, and death. The puzzle was not complete, but the edges were beginning to take shape. Faith's death... Paul's desperation. There was more than met the eye in this grim puzzle.

In the eerie silence of a roller rink, a man named Clarence met his startling end by a trident, pulling Detective Winston into a web of enmity and suspicion involving two unusual suspects, Unity and Vivian.

"What brings you here, detective?" Unity stood up from the front desk of the maritime museum, the cold light accentuating her already pale complexion.

"I hope you haven't come to see the tridents, the tour just ended," she said, holding up a ring of keys that jingled delicately. "As the tour guide here, I'm the only one with keys to the exhibits and I’ve had quite the training in handling and explaining these tridents."

Detective Winston nodded casually, taking in the details of Unity's surroundings. "Interesting set of keys you got there. You’ve got quite a bit of unrestricted access, huh?".

"Well, one of the perks of the job." Unity shrugged, her gaze resting confidently on the detective.

"Speaking of jobs, detective," she said, gesturing towards a leaflet on the table that detailed the different types of tridents. "Having spent years getting certified to handle these ancient artifacts, I now explain about these tridents as part of my daily routine. Not everyone can do that."

The detective couldn't help but notice Unity's slight smirk. "I can imagine," Winston replied casually. "This kind of specialized training demands skill, doesn’t it?"

Unity chuckled at that. "Indeed, it does..."

“The roller rink, it’s not too far from here, is it?” Detective Winston asked, pointing down the street.

"No, just a short walk. It's practically on the same street as us," Unity confirmed, her tone cautious now. "I was there earlier today, right after completing my last tour and just before the dreadful incident happened. I didn't notice anything unusual."

Detective Winston gave her a non-committal nod, his attention now elsewhere as he studied a photo held at an angle, the light catching a face he knew too well. "Ah, Clarence?” Unity's frozen nod and dead stare confirmed his suspicion. The victim had been convinced Unity was a fraud, publicly threatening to expose the loopholes in her supposedly comprehensive knowledge on maritime history just before his untimely murder.

Unity was proud, her reputation meant everything to her.

Winston's eyes returned to Unity, her face pale under the museum's poor lighting. He had nothing concrete that could tie Unity to the murder, but the pieces were falling into place.

“Well, Unity, thank you for your time,” Winston concluded as he left the museum, leaving Unity alone among the ancient displays and echoing silence.

Winston was sitting down in a neon-lit roller rink, his tired eyes soaking in the scene of Clarence's unusual murder. No leads except for one: Vivian, a vendor who worked in the rink. He'd heard rumors about her past, her fascination with historical warfare, and her penchant for sprinkling violent movie quotes during conversations. 

He had heard from the other vendors in the roller rink, how they found her behavior disconcerting, especially during meetings when she'd regale them with dialogues from brutal, blood-soaked films. Not just that, she was known to have an unnerving love for these violent movies, a fact confirmed by countless customers who recounted their conversations with her. 

Winston knew Vivian had a sister. A sister who once confided in her about Clarence's inappropriate messages. Vivian, with her history of being fiercely protective of her sister – once even taking on a bully who bothered the little girl - perceived Clarence's behavior as a threat.

With all this knowledge, Winston decided he should go and meet up with Vivian. It wasn't a short ride; he had to traverse the half-lit, mostly deserted city. But, it was necessary.

As he knocked on Vivian's front door, anxiety crept over him. He didn't know what to expect.

"Hello, Detective," Vivian greeted him after opening the door. Her house was filled with vintage items, among which was a trident, an artifact Winston couldn't help but notice. "Yes, I'm a bit of a relic collector myself," Vivian confessed.

They talked about her job at the rink, her colleagues, and much to Winston's astonishment, she even mentioned attending a trident handling course last summer. Vivian's passionate recall of her past as a historian specializing in ancient warfare left a lasting impression. 

The conversation shifted to more personal matters. As Winston learned more about her family, Vivian confirmed that her sister was indeed her last living relative. She recounted about how she defended her sister against bullies in the past and how she was in an uncomfortable position due to Clarence's intrusive behavior.

Winston asked, "Clarence used to come around a lot, didn't he?" Vivian's face turned stiff, "Yes, he did. Always with the same routine. Always bothering my sister non-stop."

"Well, someone poisoned the well, didn't they?" Vivian quoted, sounding like a character from one of her favorite films. Winston left her in silence, leaving her own words as a cryptic closure. 

As he exited, Winston felt a shiver run down his spine. Exiting the lonesome house and her world of historical artifacts and violent movie quotes, he couldn't shake off the eeriness of Vivian’s world. 

Finally, Winston drove off, leaving Vivian's historical artifact-filled refuge behind, the chilling quotes from violent movies reverberating in his ears.

In the shimmering opulence of a luxury restaurant, Roderick's life was abruptly ended by a pistol's merciless blow; now Detective Winston must untangle the web of Oscar and Brianna's testimonies.

Detective Winston, staring at the rain streaming down his office window, absentmindedly stirred his lukewarm coffee. Another murder landed on his desk. The victim, Roderick. The list of facts pertaining to Brianna, a tenacious teacher suspected to be involved, seemed to be a never-ending stream of potential leads.

Sifting through stacks of evidence, he came across a statement from Roderick, Brianna's boss, refusing to consider her for a promotion at work. Winston placed it on top of the pile as he planned his approach. The next piece of evidence was a statement from a valet at the luxury restaurant. According to the valet, not only did both Brianna and Roderick dine there on the night of the murder, but they were also both seen leaving the restaurant at the same time.

Winston made his way over to the shooting range. A police report detailed that a pistol Brianna recently purchased and practiced with here was identical to the one used to kill Roderick. 

The shooting range was winding down for the evening. Winston was able to speak to the range officer, "So, Brianna's been coming here often?"

"Yeah, she's really dedicated. You wouldn't believe it but she's won several competitions here," the range officer commented, leading Winston to the lanes where Brianna often practiced.

Within his stack of evidence, Winston found a copy of the restaurant's reservation list, confirming Brianna's presence at Classico's that night. More evidence from his stack showed that Brianna had been ambitiously seeking the same promotion at the school she worked, the promotion Roderick instead received.

He soon found himself speaking with the restaurant staff. The valet, waitstaff, and even some kitchen staff all recalled seeing Brianna leave the restaurant around the same time as Roderick. Most interestingly, they all bore witness to an argument that Brianna had with Roderick during dinner.

Next, Winston stopped by the school where Roderick worked. A fellow teacher revealed how deeply disappointed Brianna was when Roderick got the promotion instead of her.

With the collected evidence, Winston knew he needed to confront Brianna. 

"We've talked to the range officer at the shooting range," said Winston, meeting Brianna in her classroom.

Brianna nodded, "Yes, I spill my frustrations on paper targets, helps me to stay focused."

"Do you dine at Classico's often," Winston asked casually.

"Yes, once every so often," replied Brianna, "I’m a regular there."

"I’m sure they recognized you the night Roderick was killed," Winston said, subtly sliding the copy of the reservations list across the desk. 

"I suppose," Brianna said, cleaning her glasses, "But isn’t it a little strange that a busy detective like you is asking about dinner plans?”

Winston shrugged and stood up. "Well, duty calls. It was nice chatting with you, Brianna." Making his leave, Winston thought about all the pieces he had gathered and how they all seemed to point to Brianna.

Winston was nursing a black coffee and flipping through the case file when the first cracks of dawn speckled the dreary sky. The victim, Roderick, had been a stand-up entrepreneur before he caught a bullet. Roderick had agreed to meet his husband, Oscar, to discuss their divorce plans on the day he died. 

"Why flee when you're already getting a divorce?" Winston found himself murmuring to his empty, scarcely lit office. A note from a confidential source in the case file revealed that Oscar had heard from Roderick that he was planning to leave him. 

Winston's musings were interrupted by a phone call. It was Oscar's son, Josh. He cheerfully announced his excitement about the languid summer that lay ahead of him, spent at home. Winston rubbed his eyes, cracked his back, and decided it was time to pay Oscar a visit.

Oscar lived in a modest suburban home. The early morning dew lightly wet the sidewalk and the chill hung in the air. His silver sedan with premium rims was parked in the driveway, just as Oscar's neighbor had mentioned. She'd been seeing their car parked there with the windows down at all times lately. Upon inspection, Winston could see a receipt for a large, black suitcase on the passenger seat. He made a note of it.

Oscar, on the other hand, looked like a shadow of his former self. Tired eyes, unkempt hair, and the flicker of sadness in his eyes confirmed his ongoing love for Roderick, despite everything. The sad fact that he had been forced to say goodbye to his job a month ago only added to his woe. His therapist had been supporting him through the divorce-related depression, but with Roderick's sudden demise, things had taken a turn for the worse.

Winston was offered a cup of coffee while he casually asked Oscar about the night of Roderick's death. Oscar offered up the information that he had proposed a toast at the private party right before Roderick was shot, diverting everyone's attentions momentarily away from the man. After having his fill of the tepid liquid, Winston got up, thanked Oscar for his time, and walked back towards his car.

The sound of his shoes crunching the freshly dewed gravel, Winston lit up a cigarette. He drove away eventually, leaving Oscar in his rearview mirror, standing in the doorway. He gave an inward groan thinking about the mountain of paperwork waiting for him at the station.

In this mess, a voice echoed in his head, 'Heard Oscar was in therapy. Depression, they said.' 

It was a long day and Winston was certain, it was going to be a long case.

Target case file:

In the hushed sanctity of a mosque, Kent falls victim to a deadly snake venom, leaving Detective Winston with two prime suspects: Ronald and Julia.

Winston parked outside the museum, wiping a sweat off his brow as he observed the row of windows facing the parking lot. The mystery of Kent's death was still lingering, and it had become clear that he had to delve further into the details than anticipated.

Walking into the complex building, the detective stopped outside the Herpetarium where Julia currently worked. Julia once mentioned offhandedly, "I trained as a herpetologist, that's my background." He stared at the array of snakes - some small, some dangerously large, but all housed carefully in glass terrariums. Julia was in the midst of handling one of the sizeable serpents, its scales reflecting the light in an almost hypnotic way.

"Julia?" He questioned, gaining her attention.

"That's me," she affirmed, gently placing the snake back into its tank.

"Mind if we talk a moment?"

"I've got nothing to hide," the woman replied as she led him back behind her desk, scattered with numerous manuals and books about programming and tech innovations. A receptionist's post-it came from nowhere and stuck to her palm, "Remember: Staff Meeting. Introduce Julia – New Software Engineer." She rolled her eyes and said, "I'm now working as a software engineer." An out-of-place office notification chimed and she shrugged.

"Did you know about the info posted on the company's Facebook page yesterday?" He asked. She shook her head, adding, "I never keep up with that. Too busy with my work, you see. Truthfully, I don't even have a Facebook account of my own."

"Do you visit the mosque nearby?" He questioned. She nodded. 

"Why, yes, I do. I was there with my cousin Kent the same day before..." her voice wavered. "We had a disagreement. People saw us arguing," she added.

She escorted Winston to her home soon after, where a vial of snake venom sat on her coffee table.

"Why do you have that?" He asked, looking at the vial but careful not to touch.

"I work with venomous snakes, detective," she said, a matter of factly tone threading her voice. "Research." 

They had coffee in silence after that. Interesting, he thought as he left her house. He had a lot more work to do.

As Winston tied his shoe, a fellow cop whistled. He didn’t need to look up to know what was coming up next.

"Did you know snake venom can be lethal?" said the officer as he stepped aside to let a group of zookeepers from the local zoo, renowned for its variety of venomous snakes, carry a large reticulated python past.

"Yeah, interesting creatures, snakes," replied Winston without breaking stride. He continued toward the office door where a zoo security guard profile was awaiting him, the guard whose shift happened to line up with the time of the Kent's death at the mosque.

As he was flipping through the guard’s file, he noticed the man’s name, Ronald. He was a unique type of security, it seems - besides patrolling the mosque during prayer hours, he also worked at the zoo, and one of his main duties involved handling the zoo's assortment of dangerous animals, including venomous snakes. God knows there were too many types of them at that zoo.

His phone rang. It was the Imam.

"Detective Winston, Kent was here for prayers daily, he was very religious," he said when Winston picked up.

Winston thanked the Imam and hung up, then got up and headed to the mosque. Ronald worked during prayer hours which meant he could've seen Kent arriving or leaving.

Kent was there pretty much every day. There was no way for Ronald to miss seeing Kent on his death day.

After arriving at the mosque, Winston saw Ronald standing guard. He prepared himself for the hard part of his job - accusations and denials.

"Ronald, we found these," Winston showed Ronald the documents found in Kent's possession. The paperwork portrayed previous indictments, some acquittals, some convictions. Ronald's entire criminal record laid bare on papers.

"What the hell do you want?" Ronald's face turned red, and he grunted vehemently. "I have nothing to do with those papers!"

Knowing better, Winston didn't continue this line of questioning and instead took a more amiable approach. "So, you are also a snake keeper at the zoo, Ronald?"

Ronald's red face softened, and he seemed slightly less tense. "Yes, I do. I have the keys to all the enclosures, from the common rattlesnakes to the deadly cobras." Maybe it was the change of topic, maybe it was the sense of the authority that these keys brought him, but Ronald was less defensive now.

Winston nodded, thanked Ronald for his time, then turned his back towards him, leaving Ronald alone with the darkening facade of the mosque and a bag of anxiety.
